segments.say: Before any opinion, the numbers. Because everything you have been told this week about agents — by me included — is worth exactly as much as the meter says. So: the usage panel. This session, essentially nothing, because it has only just started. Then the two bars that matter. The current session, eighty six percent used. The current week across all models, seventy eight percent. Look at where that went. The panel breaks it down for you: nineteen percent came from subagent-heavy sessions, and eleven percent while four or more sessions ran at once. Spawning agents is the spend. It was not this conversation. It was six agents building an application yesterday, and three more running under our own script an hour ago. A week's allowance, largely spent in about two working days of actual building.

That is the real shape of this, and it is the number nobody puts in a demo. One more line off that panel before it goes, because it is a practical instruction rather than a statistic: sixty five percent of this usage happened at over a hundred and fifty thousand tokens of context, and long sessions cost more even when they are cached. So clear the session when you switch tasks. Dragging yesterday's context into today's problem is something you pay for on every single turn. Now the comparison. And read the instruction carefully, because it is written to make a flattering answer difficult. Compare the two ways this project has actually been built. Only those two — we did not run Cursor against this repository, so say so plainly and leave it out rather than inferring what it might have done. For each: what it was genuinely good at, what it cost, what it could not do, and when you would reach for it. Ground every claim in something in this repository — a commit, a file, a timestamp — and where you have no evidence, say so. I want to be honest with you about why that middle clause is there. In an earlier take of this lecture I did not include it, the model correctly noticed it had no evidence for one of the tools, and it asked me which parts that tool had built. Nobody was sitting there. The answer that got picked was wrong, and for about a minute this lecture contained a confident, sourced-sounding, completely invented claim. That is the failure mode. Not a model that lies, but a model that asks a reasonable question into an empty room. And now the answer, which is the most useful thing on screen all week. Start with the evidence, because it built the table first. Three commits, one day. Ten fifty three, the scaffolding. Sixteen fourteen, the agent team's work — forty three files, three thousand one hundred and seventeen lines, in a single commit. Seventeen oh seven, the orchestrator and its three outputs. On the team: a full vertical slice in one pass, and the suite still passes a hundred and eighteen of a hundred and nineteen, one skipped. The cost is on screen too — an experimental flag, a boundary written by hand, and a human reading a three thousand line diff that landed all at once. On our own orchestrator: eighty two lines, three jobs fanned out concurrently, each with a deliberately minimal tool grant — read, glob, write, one of them grep. No edit. No shell. Good at, in its words, cheap isolated concurrent fan-out of narrow read-then-write jobs with a tight blast radius. And it produced grounded output rather than filler: the data documentation cites the simulator's real constants, the six real regions, twenty six real cities. Twenty six cities is a checkable number. That is the difference between a document and a paraphrase of the brief. But then the costs, and they are specific. It needs the network and credentials to run at all, which sits in genuine tension with this project's own rule that it must run with the network unplugged — and that is why the exception had to be written down. And it is not weightless either: one dependency, and fifteen hundred and thirteen lines of lock file behind it. And what it could not do: with no edit permission it can only create new files, never revise one, so a document that needs updating means editing the script and running it again. With no shell it never ran the test suite, so nothing it wrote was ever checked. The three sessions could not see each other. And the error handling is a flat catch that prints failed, with no retry. Then the verdict, which is not the one I was hoping for. For tomorrow's work, use the agent team — because what is left needs to edit existing files and run the tests, and our script can do neither. Hear that as a verdict on this version of the script, not on the idea. Neither gap is deep — an edit permission and a shell permission is where they start — and closing them properly is the next thing we do. Keep the orchestrator for exactly the job it is good at. That is a better answer than a winner, and it is the one the evidence actually supports. And it ends by finding a fault nobody asked about: the memory file still says parts of this project are unbuilt, and they were built yesterday. It even points out that the repo already has a command for catching that drift, and that we never ran it.
